system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2169-10-15 18:42:00 to 2169-10-18 16:46:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A young woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia, laryngeal stenosis, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and tracheostomy dependence was admitted for evaluation of worsening dysphagia and odynophagia. She reported a three-day history of sore throat and difficulty swallowing, with coughing after liquids. Initial workup showed normal labs and a clear chest X-ray. Speech and swallow evaluation revealed improved swallowing with tracheostomy occlusion, and an EGD showed no mechanical obstruction. Her symptoms were attributed to pharyngeal residue, and she was successfully managed with behavioral strategies. She tolerated a regular diet with technique modification, remained stable, and was discharged home with follow-up instructions.
problems: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia originating in the perinatal period
Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified

Discharge Instructions:
Dear Ms. ___,

It was our pleasure taking care of you at the ___ 
___!

WHY WERE YOU ADMITTED TO THE HOSPITAL?
- You were having difficulty swallowing at home and had throat 
pain, especially with swallowing.

WHAT HAPPENED IN THE HOSPITAL?
- You were seen by the Interventional Pulmonologists, who 
determined that your tracheostomy was in the right place and 
your swallowing issues were not related to it.
- You were seen by the Otolaryngologists who performed endoscopy 
at the bedside. This did not find an explanation for your 
swallowing issues.
- You were seen by the Speech Language Pathologists, who helped 
you work on strategies to improve your swallowing. They felt 
that you were safe to resume a normal diet.
- You underwent a video swallow, which did not show any 
aspiration of food contents into your airways.
- You underwent a barium swallow, which showed that you had 
moderate esophageal dysmotility, meaning your esophagus does not 
move as it normally should.
- You were provided pain control and given IV fluids until you 
were able to resume a regular diet.

WHAT SHOULD YOU DO ONCE YOU LEAVE THE HOSPITAL?
- Please take all your medications as prescribed and attend all 
your doctor's appointments.
- Please continue to work on the swallowing techniques you 
developed with the help of the Speech therapists, which includes 
3 swallows with 1 solid food bolus, 2 swallows with 1 liquid 
food bolus, and occluding trach with each food bolus to improve 
swallowing pressure and bolus flow.
- Please see a gastroenterologist about the esophageal 
dysmotility. You can arrange this appointment through your 
primary doctor.
- Please be conscious of your diet. Your blood sugars were high 
in the hospital, meaning that you may have diabetes. You should 
see your primary doctor about this.

We wish you all the best!
Your ___ Healthcare Team

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been having trouble swallowing again—like food gets stuck in my throat. It hurts, especially when I try to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And does it happen more with solids or liquids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mostly solids. I haven’t eaten anything today because it just hurts too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You mentioned pain—does it hurt only when you swallow, or is there a constant soreness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s there all the time, but worse when I swallow. I feel like I’m choking, and I’m scared I might aspirate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds really distressing. I know you’ve had this before—last time, they thought it was due to residue in your throat and gave you some swallowing techniques.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they said to cover my trach when I swallow. But I also remember being told to tuck my chin. It’s hard to do both at once.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll get the speech team to help you with that again. For now, we’ll keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—until we figure things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I’m just worried this is something new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve checked your labs and chest X-ray. Everything looks stable—no infection, no lung issues. Your trach site looks clean too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my trach causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The interventional pulmonology team saw you and said your trach is fine. They don’t think it’s the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The ENT team did a bedside scope yesterday. They saw some nasal swelling and a deviated septum, but nothing that explains your swallowing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain and the feeling of food getting stuck?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still working on that. You’re scheduled for a video swallow test today—that’ll show us how your throat and esophagus are moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not painful. You’ll swallow some barium-coated foods while they take X-ray videos. It helps us see if food is going where it should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, just got the results from your video swallow. Good news—no aspiration. You’re not breathing food into your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But why do I keep coughing after I swallow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The speech team noticed that too. But on the video, there was no food in your airway. They think it’s due to throat sensitivity—your nerves are a bit overreacting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So I’m safe to eat?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they think you can start a regular diet. But we’ll make sure you use the swallowing techniques—like covering your trach—to help things move smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But can we go over the steps again? I keep forgetting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. For solids: take one bite, then swallow three times. For liquids: two swallows per sip. And cover your trach with your finger each time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And what about the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you Tylenol and ibuprofen. They should help. We’re also checking your blood sugar because it was high this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High sugar? I don’t have diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily, but your fasting sugars have been in the 160s–170s. We checked your A1c, and it’s 7.9, which suggests prediabetes or early diabetes. We’ll talk more about that before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got the barium swallow results. It shows moderate esophageal dysmotility—your esophagus isn’t squeezing food down as well as it should.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why food feels stuck?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be contributing. We didn’t see this before, so it might be new. We recommend seeing a gastroenterologist after discharge to look into it further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s manageable. It may explain your symptoms, and there are treatments. But for now, you’re doing well—you’ve been eating without trouble, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, actually. The pain is much better, and I haven’t choked once since I started using the technique.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep you on ibuprofen for pain and make sure you stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using the swallowing techniques. Follow up with ENT in four weeks, and please see a gastroenterologist about the esophageal motility issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—talk to your primary doctor about that. Lifestyle changes may help, but you might need medication. We’ve included all this in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Keep up the good work with your swallowing, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The speech therapist will come by one more time to review the technique before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’d be helpful. I want to get this right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. You’re doing great. We’re confident you’ll do well at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad I came in. I was really worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was the right call. We found some new things, and now we have a plan. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A young woman with a history of tracheobronchomalacia, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, and tracheostomy dependence was admitted for recurrent dysphagia and throat pain. She reported food sticking and odynophagia, with no recent oral intake. Initial evaluation showed no acute findings on labs or chest imaging. ENT evaluation revealed no structural cause, and a video swallow study showed no aspiration but frequent post-swallow coughing likely due to hypersensitivity. A barium swallow revealed moderate esophageal dysmotility, a new finding. She was advanced to a regular diet with improved symptoms using swallowing techniques involving trach occlusion. Pain was controlled with acetaminophen and ibuprofen. Hyperglycemia was noted with an A1c of 7.9, prompting outpatient follow-up. She was discharged home in stable condition with plans to see ENT, gastroenterology, and her primary care provider for diabetes evaluation.
